item: Which year a patent belongs to
precedent: Hall, Jaffe & Trajtenberg (2001, NBER WP 8498) date patents by application year; Katila & Ahuja (2002); Gilsing et al. (2008)

reason: USPC is no longer kept up to date. Same choice as P023
precedent: CPC and IPC are identical at four characters (Leydesdorff, Kogler & Yan 2017)

options: the four-character CPC subclass of the first-listed code; the subclasses of all codes on the patent; the finer CPC group
choice: The four-character CPC subclass of the first-listed code. All codes as a robustness check
reason: Same as P023, one class per patent. Pouya chose the level on 18 Oct. The four-character subclass stands for the same idea as the old USPC main class, the patent's technology area, though the two systems have different sets of classes (about 420 to 470 USPC main classes against 654 CPC subclasses in use). Published use of four-character IPC or CPC subclasses as technology classes is enough precedent, so this project doesn't compare USPC and CPC. Pouya recalls the two giving close results in P023 (not rechecked here). The first-listed code takes the place of the single original USPC class that the NBER data used. Check on 30 Oct: the first-listed code is marked "additional" rather than inventional for 902 of the 1,738,450 patents in the sample. Using each patent's first inventional code changes new_classes in 47 of 157,180 firm-years, so the first-listed code stays
precedent: Level: four-character IPC or CPC subclasses in Belderbos et al. (2010), Lerner (1994), Leydesdorff et al. (2017: 654 CPC subclasses in use). Codes: all classes recommended by Benner & Waldfogel (2008) and used by Leten et al. (2016); the first or original class used by Hall, Jaffe & Trajtenberg (2001), Vanhaverbeke et al. (2009), Balsmeier et al. (2017). The USPTO names one first CPC code per patent (MPEP 905). Literature check (30 Oct): the USPTO rule makes the first CPC symbol "the inventive classification symbol which most adequately represents the invention as a whole" (MPEP 905.03(a)). Benner & Waldfogel (2008) find most research uses only the first class and call all classes conceptually preferable. One class per patent for new-class measures: Manso, Balsmeier & Fleming (working paper), Ganco, Miller & Toh (2020). All classes: Leten, Belderbos & Van Looy (2016), Jiang, Tan & Thursby (2011), Arts & Fleming (2018)
decided_by: Pouya (level, 18 Oct; first-listed code, 30 Oct after the literature check)

options: base t-5 to t-1 and forward t to t+2; base t-5 to t-1 and forward t+1 to t+3; other lengths
choice: base t-5 to t-1, forward t to t+2
reason: A five-year base and a three-year forward window are common choices for search measures. On 18 Oct Pouya set the lengths (five years back, three years forward). Where year t goes was Claude's proposal, built as a provisional choice and left open for his review as D10. On 30 Oct he decided the forward window starts in year t
precedent: Base t-5 to t-1: Belderbos et al. (2010), word for word; Gilsing et al. (2008); Vanhaverbeke et al. (2009); Leten et al. (2016). Three years starting with t: Lee, Park & Kang (2018) count over t to t+2; Mealey, Koka & Hoskisson (2025) over t to t+2; Gilsing et al. (2008) and Belderbos et al. (2010) let a class keep its explorative status for three years from its entry year t

item: Firm-years with no patents in the base window
options: missing; zero; count every forward class as new
reason: Without a base there is nothing to compare against, so there is no value
precedent: Units without earlier patents treated as not at risk: Arts & Fleming (2018); Belderbos et al. (2010) restrict the sample the same way; Lerner & Seru (2021)

reason: Usable patent data starts in 1982, so the first full five-year base is 1982-1986 and the first focal year is 1987. The forward window has to end by 2018, because many applications filed after that were still waiting for a decision when the data were drawn. With the forward window at t to t+2 (D10), 2016 would also have a full forward window, and the focal years stay 1987-2015
precedent: Hall, Jaffe & Trajtenberg (2001) leave a three-year gap at the end when patents are dated by application year

reason: The rule used in the researcher's pipeline

options: one worked case walked through the code by the researcher; 10, 30 or 100+ random cases worked by hand
choice: One worked case: a real firm-year traced step by step through the slow version and the definition (handcheck/walkthrough.R). The random worksheet (100 or more random cases and about 10 tricky ones, windows unmarked) stays in the repository as a tool for Stage 2
reason: Pouya, 18 Oct 2026. The hand-check means reviewing the code once with one set of numbers, and the 100-case version came from a misunderstanding. The three separate versions already agree on every firm-year
precedent: Rule of three for the Stage 2 random sample: Hanley & Lippman-Hand (1983)

options: in neither window (base t-5 to t-1, forward t+1 to t+3); in the forward window (base t-5 to t-1, forward t to t+2); in the base (base t-4 to t, forward t+1 to t+3)
choice: in the forward window: base t-5 to t-1, forward t to t+2, so the two windows touch
reason: Pouya, 30 Oct 2026: the firm looks at its previous five years and moves in the three years that follow, starting with t, and no year can fall between the two windows. A literature check the same day found that every confirmed paper ends the base in the year just before the new-activity window, usually a base of t-5 to t-1 with new activity in t, and none leaves a gap year. The earlier rule, with year t in neither window, had no precedent
precedent: Gilsing et al. (2008); Belderbos et al. (2010); Leten, Belderbos & Van Looy (2016); Manso, Balsmeier & Fleming (working paper); Ganco, Miller & Toh (2020); Gao, Hsu & Li (2018, JFQA), new patents t-2 to t against a base of t-7 to t-3; Derayati (2026, BJM)

item: Which owner a patent links to (public build)
options: A: the owner DISCERN records for the application at filing, or if there is none, the owner of the matched name on the grant in the calendar year of filing; B: the owner DISCERN's grant file records at the grant year; C: the links from the researcher's own pipeline, which need licensed Compustat data
choice: A, with B built as a robustness check
reason: A follows the researcher's own pipeline in every step but one. The pipeline dates the link by each firm's fiscal year, which needs licensed Compustat data, and A uses the calendar year. C can't be shared. Compared with the researcher's own pipeline (report/link_agreement_*.csv), A links 99.8% of patents filed 1982-2018 to the same firm or firms, and B links 89.0%
